Chapter 2: Transformer Mechanics & The Attention Tax: Math Don't Lie

If you think the problem with JSON is just paying too much to your cloud provider, you're missing the entire technical failure mode. The financial bleed is just the receipt; the crime scene is happening inside the model’s attention heads.

Every self-proclaimed "AI Engineer" loves to wave their hands and talk about "emergent reasoning," but none of them actually look at the tensor operations executing on the GPU clusters. Let's look at the actual mathematics of scaled dot-product attention in modern Transformer architectures:

$$\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V$$

Here:

  • $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d_k}$ is the Query projection of sequence length $N$ and dimension $d_k$.
  • $K \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d_k}$ is the Key projection of sequence length $N$.
  • $V \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d_v}$ is the Value projection containing the semantic embeddings.
  • $N$ is the sequence length in tokens.

Notice that term in the middle: $Q K^T$. That produces an $N \times N$ attention weight matrix.

$$\text{Complexity} = \mathcal{O}(N^2)$$

When you feed an LLM an $N$-token sequence, every single token computes a dot product with every other token in the sequence across every single attention head in every layer. If your sequence has 10,000 tokens, your model computes 100,000,000 attention scores per head, per layer.

Chapter 3: The L1 Cache Crime Scene: Heap Thrashing vs. Spatial Contiguity

Most web developers think RAM is just a magic infinite bucket where you dump variables and the computer figures it out. They have zero understanding of the physical memory hierarchy, cache line sizes, or how CPU prefetchers actually fetch instructions from silicon.

Let's educate the noobs.

A modern server CPU (whether an AMD EPYC, Intel Xeon, or Apple/ARM64 Neoverse core) does not read memory byte-by-byte from your 64GB DDR5 stick. That would take ~60 to 100 nanoseconds per read—an eternity in computing time. Instead, the CPU features a tiered cache architecture:

  • L1 Data Cache: ~32KB to 64KB per core, ~1 nanosecond latency (4–5 cycles).
  • L2 Cache: ~512KB to 1MB per core, ~3 to 4 nanoseconds latency (14 cycles).
  • L3 Cache: Shared 32MB to 256MB, ~10 to 15 nanoseconds latency (40–50 cycles).
  • Main DRAM: Off-chip silicon, ~60 to 100 nanoseconds latency (200+ cycles).

Every time your program reads a pointer from main memory that isn't already sitting in the L1/L2 cache, the CPU pipeline halts. It stalls. It sits there doing nothing for 200 clock cycles waiting for the memory controller to drag the bytes across the physical motherboard traces.

  5. Every single string key (e.g. "server_node_id", "timestamp_iso") is allocated as its own independent PyASCIIObject or PyCompactUnicodeObject on the heap (48–80 bytes each!).

The Spatial Prefetcher Miracle

Modern CPUs contain dedicated hardware units called Stream Prefetchers (or Spatial Prefetchers).

When the prefetcher detects that your program is accessing memory at linear, predictable stride intervals (Address, Address + 8, Address + 16, Address + 24), it doesn't wait for your code to request the next row. It speculatively streams the next 4 to 8 cache lines from DRAM directly into the L1 data cache ahead of time!

  • Under standard JSON: The CPU jumps to random heap locations. The stream prefetcher cannot predict where the next dictionary lives. Prefetching fails completely. Every read is a DRAM penalty.
  • Under BEJSON 104a: The Values array is a clean, sequential matrix. The prefetcher locks on instantly. By the time your serialization loop finishes processing Row 0, Row 1 and Row 2 are already sitting warm in the L1 cache.

export interface BEJSONEnvelope<TValues = any[]> {
  Format: 'BEJSON';
  Format_Version: '104' | '104a' | '104db' | '105' | '105a';
  Format_Creator: string;
  Records_Type: string[];
  Fields: BEJSONField[];
  Values: TValues[];
}

export type FieldMap = Record<string, number>;

export class BEJSONEngine<TRecord extends Record<string, any>> {
  private fieldMap: FieldMap;

  constructor(public doc: BEJSONEnvelope) {
    this.fieldMap = this.compileFieldMap();
  }

  private compileFieldMap(): FieldMap {
    const map: FieldMap = {};
    this.doc.Fields.forEach((field, index) => {
      map[field.name] = index;
    });
    return map;
  }

  public getRecord(rowIndex: number): TRecord | null {
    const row = this.doc.Values[rowIndex];
    if (!row) return null;
    const record: any = {};
    for (const [key, colIdx] of Object.entries(this.fieldMap)) {
      record[key] = row[colIdx];
    }
    return record as TRecord;
  }

  public getField<K extends keyof TRecord>(rowIndex: number, fieldName: K): TRecord[K] {
    const colIdx = this.fieldMap[fieldName as string];
    if (colIdx === undefined) {
      throw new Error(`Field '${String(fieldName)}' not found in schema.`);
    }
    return this.doc.Values[rowIndex][colIdx];
  }
}

bejson_get_field_index() {

    in_fields && /"Values":/ { in_fields = 0; }

      idx++;
    }
    END { print found; }
  ' "$file"

bejson_query_column() {

  local file="$1"
  local target_field="$2"
  local col_idx
  
  col_idx=$(bejson_get_field_index "$file" "$target_field")
  if [ "$col_idx" -lt 0 ]; then
    echo "ERROR: Field '$target_field' not found in BEJSON schema." >&2
    return 1

    in_values && /^\s*\[/ {
      # Strip brackets and whitespace
      line = $0;
      gsub(/[\[\]]/, "", line);
      split(line, cells, ",");
      gsub(/^[ \t]+|[ \t]+$/, "", cells[col]);
      gsub(/^"|"$/, "", cells[col]);
      if (cells[col] != "") {
        print cells[col];
      }
    }
  ' "$file"
